events.title: Staples dumped for internet stocks in 1999, then rebought as the 'old economy' refuge

events.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act cuts Medicaid by about $1 trillion
events.summary: The OBBBA, signed July 4 2025, imposes 80-hour monthly work requirements, six-monthly eligibility checks, a provider-tax cap falling from 6% to 3.5% by 2031 and tighter retroactive coverage, cutting federal Medicaid/CHIP funding by roughly $1 trillion over ten years; CBO estimated about 10 million more uninsured by 2034 (10.9 million for the House version), partly offset by a $50 billion rural hospital fund. Hospital operators and Medicaid managed-care insurers (Centene, Molina) carry the exposure, with most provisions phasing in from 2027.

events.title: OBBBA terminates EV tax credits after September 30 2025
events.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act ended the $7,500 new and $4,000 used clean-vehicle credits for purchases after September 30 2025 and the charging-property credit after June 2026. The deadline produced a Q3 2025 EV sales pull-forward followed by a demand cliff in Q4, hitting Rivian, Lucid and the EV programs of GM and Ford, while Tesla's exposure was partly offset by its robotaxi and AI narrative.

events.title: OBBBA cuts SNAP by $186 billion
events.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act extends SNAP work requirements to ages 18-64, shifts up to 15% of benefit costs and 75% of administration costs to states and restricts Thrifty Food Plan updates, reducing federal nutrition funding by $186 billion over 2025-2034. SNAP is a meaningful share of sales at dollar stores, discount grocers and Walmart and of volumes for packaged-food makers, so the law is a slow-burning headwind for the lower-income staples channel from 2026.

events.title: Shutdown fight over expiring enhanced ACA subsidies
events.summary: The enhanced ACA premium tax credits from the 2021 American Rescue Plan, extended by the IRA, were set to expire at the end of 2025; the dispute drove a federal shutdown that passed 39 days in early November 2025. KFF found insurers proposing a median 18% premium increase for 2026 (versus 7% a year earlier), citing the expiration, with warnings that premiums could more than double for some enrollees and enrollment could fall. Exchange-heavy insurers (Oscar, Centene) and hospitals with high exchange mix carried the risk into 2026.

events.title: Supreme Court strikes down IEEPA tariffs; importers rally
events.summary: On February 20 2026 the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, voiding the 'Liberation Day' reciprocal and fentanyl tariffs (Section 232 and 301 duties were untouched). Consumer discretionary rose about 1% on the day with Amazon, Etsy, Tapestry and Williams-Sonoma up, and apparel names popped because roughly 60% of applied apparel/footwear tariffs were IEEPA-based (Morgan Stanley). The administration replaced them with a 10% Section 122 global tariff from February 24, and the Court of International Trade ordered refunds on April 20 2026, a cash windfall for importers like G-III.

events.title: Section 232 proclamation: 100% tariffs on patented drugs, with deal exemptions
events.summary: A Section 232 proclamation imposed 100% tariffs on patented (Orange/Purple Book) drugs and their APIs, with 15% for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, 10% or less for the UK, 20% for companies with approved onshoring plans, and exemptions for companies that signed pricing/manufacturing agreements; duties start July 31 2026 for 17 named companies and September 29 for others, and generics are exempt for now. Because the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling voided IEEPA tariffs but not Section 232, this became the binding tariff regime for pharma; companies with deals (Lilly, J&J, Pfizer) are largely shielded, European and Japanese names less so.
